# 21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1|21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/22 Concurrency and Parallelism/22 Concurrency and Parallelism|22 Concurrency and Parallelism]]

This lesson continues [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1/21.1 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 1#12. Horizontal scaling|horizontal scaling from Part 1]]. (The video was split in two only because of a recording problem.) It covers what makes horizontal scaling possible (statelessness), load balancers, scaling the database, CDNs and edge computing, asynchronous processing, microservices and serverless. It ends with rules of thumb for approaching performance work.

## 1. Statelessness: the key to horizontal scaling

Horizontal scaling runs **many instances** (A, B, C, D…) of the same backend code, and incoming requests are spread across them. That only works if the servers are **stateless**.

| | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Stateful server** | Holds data **only it** has, e.g. it remembers something about a user in its own memory or disk |
| **Stateless server** | Holds nothing exclusive. **Any** instance can handle **any** request with the same result |

The test: if you delete instance B, A + C + D must still behave **exactly the same**. Any data that must persist lives **outside** the servers, somewhere every instance can reach.

This is why horizontal scaling has to be planned "from the ground up". It affects **code**, infrastructure and the whole stack. Vertical scaling is just a bigger machine in a dashboard.

### Example: sessions

1. A user logs in; the request lands on **instance A**.
2. A creates a session, sets the session cookie, and stores the session **in its own memory** (e.g. an in-process array).
3. The next request lands on **instance B**. B has never seen that session, so it returns **401: please log in**. That's confusing and frustrating for the user.

**Fix:** store sessions in a shared store such as **Redis**, reachable by all instances. Then B can look up the session A created. (Sessions are covered in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/08 Authentication and Authorization/08 Authentication and Authorization#3. Three building blocks: sessions, JWTs, cookies|lesson 08]].)

### Example: file uploads

A user uploads a file; instance A saves it on **its own disk**. The next request lands on C, which can't find the file → error.

**Fix:** upload to **object storage** (Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, or self-hosted MinIO), which every instance can reach. (See [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/23 Object Storage Part 1/23 Object Storage Part 1|lesson 23]].)

### The rule: externalize all state

| Kind of state | Don't keep it in… | Keep it in… |
|---|---|---|
| Sessions, shared cache | Server memory | **Redis** (or another shared store) |
| Files | Server disk | **Object storage** (S3, R2, MinIO) |
| Application data | A database file on the server (e.g. SQLite) | A **central database** (PostgreSQL, Amazon RDS…) |

---

## 2. Load balancers

With several instances, something must decide **which instance gets each request**. That's the **load balancer (LB)**, a mandatory part of horizontal scaling. (See also [[Notes/Networking/Proxy vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer|Proxy vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer]].)

```text
users' browsers → internet → LOAD BALANCER → instance A / B / C
                                   ↑ responses go back the same way
```

1. All client requests go to the **load balancer**, not to servers directly.
2. The LB uses an **algorithm** to pick an instance and forwards the request.
3. The instance processes it and responds; the LB returns the response on the same HTTP connection.

The LB is a **middleman**. The interesting part is the algorithm.

---

## 3. Load-balancing algorithms

### Round robin

Send requests in **rotating order**: A, B, C, A, B, C…

It works well when:

- requests cost **roughly the same**, and
- servers have the **same capacity** (e.g. 4 GB RAM, 2 cores each).

Its weakness is that it's **blind** to request cost. Suppose:

- **Type 1:** a simple read (fetch a profile), about 200–300 ms,
- **Type 2:** expensive: an external call (e.g. Elasticsearch or an email API) **plus** a write to a big, heavily indexed table (every index must be updated on writes), about **2 s**.

If the arrival order lines up badly, round robin can keep sending the expensive requests to the **same** server until it struggles or crashes.

### Weighted round robin

Same rotation, but servers get requests in proportion to their **capacity**. If A has 8 GB / 4 cores and B and C have 4 GB / 2 cores, A gets **twice** as many requests: A, A, B, C, A, A, B, C… It's still blind to request cost.

### Least connections

Send each request to the server with the **fewest active connections**.

- An HTTP request keeps its connection **active** until the response is sent (simplified to HTTP/1.1; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex requests differently).
- Expensive requests stay active longer, so a busy server naturally gets **fewer new** requests.

Walkthrough:

1. All servers start at 0 connections. Request 1 (expensive, 2 s) → A.
2. Request 2 (cheap) → B. Request 3 (cheap) → C.
3. By the time request 4 arrives, B or C has finished (about 200 ms) and is back to 0, while A is still busy. Request 4 → B or C, **not** A.

There's also **weighted least connections**, which combines this with capacity weights.

### Others

| Algorithm | Picks the server that… |
|---|---|
| **Least response time** | Is currently responding **fastest**; struggling servers get fewer requests |
| **Resource-based** | Has the lowest **CPU/memory** usage |

The idea is always the same: some logic decides which instance gets the next request.

---

## 4. Health checks

What if instance A **crashes**? With round robin (or any algorithm), the LB keeps sending it a share of requests. Those users get **502/503** errors. Because of the rotation, the same user may succeed on one request and fail on the next, which is very frustrating.

**Health checks** fix this:

1. Alongside real traffic, the LB sends a small **test request** (e.g. `GET /health`) to every instance **regularly**, say every second.
2. A healthy instance answers **200** immediately. It's a trivial endpoint, so this adds almost no load.
3. If an instance answers with an error (e.g. 502) or doesn't answer, the LB marks it **unhealthy** and **stops sending real user traffic** to it.
4. The LB **keeps health-checking** the unhealthy instance. Once it returns 200 again, it goes back into rotation.

(Health checks also come up in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems/16 Error Handling and Fault-Tolerant Systems|lesson 16]] and [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/19 Graceful Shutdown/19 Graceful Shutdown#6. Step 1: connection draining|lesson 19]].)

---

## 5. Scaling the database: read replicas

Once state is externalized, scaling the **application** is straightforward: add servers behind the load balancer and capacity grows roughly linearly. The **database** is harder. It's the **stateful** part: it holds the data, and that data must stay **consistent**. You can't just copy it like a server.

Without changes, all those new app servers still hit **one** database server (say 4 GB RAM, 4 cores), which eventually runs out of resources.

### How read replicas work

| Role | Also called | Handles |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary** | master, parent | **All writes** (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`), and reads if needed |
| **Read replicas** | secondaries, children (older term: slaves) | **Reads only** (`SELECT`). Never write to them |

- Replicas hold a **copy** of the primary's data. The database's **replication** feature streams changes from primary to replicas (PostgreSQL, MySQL and others support this natively).
- Replicas can be placed **around the world**: primary in the US, replicas in India, Japan and so on, near app servers in those regions.

### Benefits

1. **Less load on the primary.** In many SaaS apps most queries are reads (70–90%). If replicas take those, the primary only handles the remaining writes (e.g. 30% instead of 100%).
2. **Lower latency** for users near a replica.

### The catch: consistency and replication lag

Physics limits how fast data can travel (fibre optic cables, including undersea ones). Copying a change from the US to India might take about **200 ms**. This delay is the **replication lag**.

The classic bug:

1. A user in India renames themselves from "A" to "AB" and clicks **Save**. It's a write, so it goes to the **primary** in the US and succeeds (200).
2. The frontend immediately refetches the profile. It's a read, so it goes to the **replica** in India **before** replication has finished.
3. The replica returns the **old** name "A". The app just said "saved", and now shows the old value. For payments or invoices, that kind of inconsistency can do real damage.

Ways to handle it:

- **Read-your-writes routing:** after a write to some data (e.g. the users table), route that user's next reads of it to the **primary**.
- **Track the replication lag** and make reads wait until the replica has caught up.
- **Design the frontend** to delay the refetch slightly, e.g. about 300 ms. (This is a simple workaround, not a guarantee.)

Which option you choose depends on the **trade-off** you accept. With distributed systems, the trade-off is almost always about **consistency**.

Managed providers (Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL…) make replicas a few **toggles or flags** away and handle many consistency issues for you. It's still important to understand the trade-off.

---

## 6. Scaling the database: sharding

Picture an e-commerce `orders` table with **billions** of rows. Even with an index on `user_id`, this can be slow:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 5;
```

Two problems: **query latency** on a huge table, and the need for **more database machines** to handle the request volume.

**Sharding** splits a table's rows across **several physical database instances** (shards). Each shard holds part of the data.

```text
orders (10 "rows", each standing for ~1 billion)
 ├─ Shard 1: orders from January–June
 └─ Shard 2: orders from July–December
```

- **More capacity:** two (or more) database servers handle more requests per second.
- **Faster queries:** each shard scans a smaller table.
- You can go finer, e.g. one shard per **month**.
- A **routing layer** in the backend decides which shard holds the data for each query.

### The hard part: choosing the shard key

The **shard key** is the value that decides where each row lives (here, the order date). Choosing it is tricky:

- if queries don't include the key (e.g. "all orders for user 5" when sharding by date), they may have to hit **every** shard,
- some keys create **hot shards**; for example, the current month gets nearly all new writes.

Many systems therefore shard by something queries always include, such as a user or tenant ID.

> [!note] Terms
> **Partitioning** often means splitting a table into pieces **inside one database server** (e.g. PostgreSQL table partitioning). **Sharding** usually means spreading those pieces across **different servers**. People sometimes use the words interchangeably.

---

## 7. Distributed and managed databases

The current trend (the video was recorded in December 2025) is **distributed databases** that handle sharding, replication and **distributed transactions** for you:

| Database | Notes |
|---|---|
| **PlanetScale** | MySQL-compatible, built on **Vitess** |
| **Neon** | Serverless PostgreSQL; its storage layer is written in Rust |
| **CockroachDB** | Distributed SQL (PostgreSQL-compatible) |
| **YugabyteDB** | Distributed SQL (PostgreSQL-compatible) |

### What this means in practice

- Unless you have deep database-administration expertise, **don't run your own database infrastructure**. Replication, sharding and **backups** (keeping data safe in multiple places) are all hard.
- Realistically, you pick a provider (RDS, Neon, PlanetScale…) based on features, price and team preference, sign up, get a **connection URL** with credentials, and plug it into your backend.
- You still need these concepts so you can **configure** the provider correctly: backup frequency, which regions get read replicas, how to plan sharding.

---

## 8. CDNs: caching at a global level

So far, caching has lived **inside your data centre**. **CDNs (Content Delivery Networks)** cache at a **global, geographic** level. (Basics in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/13 Caching/13 Caching#4. Network caching: CDNs|lesson 13]].)

### The physics problem

Light in **fibre optic cable** travels at roughly **200,000 km/s**, and that's the internet's speed limit.

- A user in **Tokyo** calling a server in **North Virginia** (AWS `us-east-1`, where many apps are hosted) makes a round trip of roughly **20,000 km**, which takes about **100 ms** at the speed of light in fibre. No optimization can beat that.
- And that's only the travel time. Add routing, JSON **deserialization**, business logic, database queries (50–100 ms) and external API calls (around 200 ms), and the user easily waits **500–800 ms**.

However much you optimize the database and caching, **distance** remains.

### How CDNs help

A CDN places **edge locations**, also called **PoPs (points of presence)**, close to users: Tokyo, Mumbai, Singapore… Content is cached there and served from nearby.

1. **Latency:** the trip shrinks from about 20,000 km to perhaps 100–200 km, so around **100 ms → 2–3 ms**.
2. **Load:** many requests never reach your origin server. You may need to scale horizontally less often.
3. **Security:** see below.

### What to put on a CDN

- **Static content**, the obvious starting point: JavaScript and CSS bundles, HTML files, images, videos, fonts. A built **single-page application** (e.g. React) or a static blog is typically deployed this way, instead of going through your server to an S3 bucket.
- **Some API responses**, e.g. a product catalogue that rarely changes.

When content changes, you **purge** (invalidate) it. **Cloudflare** (one of the largest CDNs) lets you tag cached content, e.g. by user ID, and purge everything with that tag when, say, that user publishes a new blog post. The next request fetches fresh content from the origin and caches it again.

### DDoS protection

In a **DDoS (distributed denial-of-service)** attack, an attacker controls a **botnet** (e.g. 20,000 malware-infected machines) and floods your server:

- without autoscaling, the server **crashes**,
- with autoscaling, it keeps spinning up instances and you get a huge **bill** (e.g. $50,000 in a day).

With a CDN like Cloudflare **in front** of your servers, all traffic passes through it first. It detects attack patterns, can challenge suspicious users with **CAPTCHAs**, and spreads even terabytes of attack traffic across its huge network, so your servers aren't overwhelmed.

---

## 9. Edge computing

### "Edge" in CDN terms

CDN nodes are called **edge nodes** because they sit at the **edge of the network**: the first point your request reaches, often placed in partnership with **ISPs** (internet service providers). Traditionally they only **serve files**: you ask for a file, they return it, with no processing.

### Edge computing

**Edge computing** means running **code** on those edge nodes: request → **some processing** → response. There are far more edge nodes than big data centres, and they're close to users, so even if the processing takes as long as on your origin server, the **round trip** is much shorter and the response feels much faster.

### Good use cases

- **Authentication checks:** a Tokyo user with an invalid session gets a **401** in about 2–3 ms from the edge, instead of after a 100 ms+ round trip to the US. The origin only sees **legitimate** requests, which cuts unnecessary traffic.
- **Personalisation:** read headers such as the browser's language (e.g. Japanese) and serve the localised version directly.
- **Validation** and **routing** (deciding which server should handle a request).

### Why not run everything at the edge?

- **Limited resources:** edge machines are small, e.g. around 1 GB RAM and one core instead of 8–16 GB.
- **Restricted runtimes:** e.g. **Cloudflare Workers** run in **V8 isolates** (the JavaScript engine from Chrome), which can't access a filesystem and restrict networking compared with a normal server.

So the edge **complements** origin servers rather than replacing them: put strategic, lightweight logic at the edge and keep the heavy work in the data centre.

---

## 10. Asynchronous processing

Unlike horizontal scaling (adopted at some user threshold), **asynchronous processing** is usually used **from day one**, because it cuts **perceived latency** so easily.

Some operations must be **synchronous**: e.g. updating a name. You can only say "saved" **after** the database write succeeds. Others don't need the user to wait.

### Example: inviting a team member

Many SaaS apps (Jira, Notion…) let you invite people to a workspace by email:

1. Check that the user isn't already in the team.
2. Insert an invite row with `status = pending`.
3. **Send the invite email** via an email provider's API (Mailchimp, SendGrid, Resend…).

| Approach | What the user waits for | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Synchronous | Steps 1–2 (about 50–100 ms) **plus** the email API (about 200–300 ms) | **~400 ms** |
| Asynchronous | Steps 1–2, then respond **200** right away; the email is sent in the background | **~100 ms** |

The user doesn't need the email to arrive before they see "invited". It also protects you when the email provider is slow or down.

### How it's built

(See [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs|lesson 14]].)

```text
server (producer) ──push job──▶ queue (Redis / RabbitMQ / Kafka…) ──▶ worker (consumer) ──▶ email API
        └─ responds to the user immediately
```

- The server is the **producer**: it pushes a **task/job** ("send invite email to X") into a **queue**.
- **Workers (consumers)** pick jobs from the queue and do them.
- Workers can run in the **same codebase** as the server, or as a **separate service** you scale independently.

### Other good candidates

- **Emails and notifications**: users don't expect them within the same millisecond.
- **Video and image processing**: after you upload a video to YouTube you can close the tab; thumbnails, HD encoding and subtitles are generated in the background, taking 10–20 minutes or more.
- **Deleting an account**: deleting a user's to-dos, categories, schedules, profile and finally the user row (in a transaction, children before the parent because of foreign keys) can take **seconds** for a long-time user with millions of rows. Synchronously, the user stares at a spinner for, say, 8 seconds. Asynchronously, do the basic checks (about 50–80 ms), respond "account deleted", log them out, and push a `delete_user` job that does the heavy deletes in the background.

### Tools

A managed Redis (e.g. **Upstash**) plus a job library such as **BullMQ** (Node.js), which uses Redis and handles error handling, retries and rate limiting.

**Step one is identifying which tasks can be offloaded**: anything whose result the user doesn't need immediately.

---

## 11. Monoliths vs microservices

### Monolith

A **monolith** is a backend deployed as **one unit**: auth, orders, notifications, payments and webhooks are just **modules** (folders/files) in **one codebase**, running in one process (or several identical processes when scaled horizontally).

It's simple to **develop**, **test** (one process), **refactor** (change several modules in one place) and **deploy**. And you can still scale a monolith horizontally.

### Microservices

**Microservices** split the backend into **independently deployable services**. Their main benefit is scaling the **team**, not the machines. Consider them when you have a **large organisation**: roughly 100–200+ developers on the same product.

Problems monoliths cause at that size:

1. **Deployment coupling:** the payments team wants to ship an urgent change, but the main branch also contains the notifications team's unfinished work. Feature flags and careful branching help (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/17 Configuration Management/17 Configuration Management#3. Types of configuration|feature flags]]), but with hundreds of loosely connected developers this keeps happening. Small startup teams (10–30 people) usually coordinate well enough to avoid it.
2. **Uneven scaling:** payments and orders need lots of CPU and memory, notifications barely any. With a monolith you must scale **everything** together. With microservices, each service scales **independently**.
3. **Different tech stacks:** a blogging platform (e.g. Medium, Hashnode, DEV) might need a Node.js or Python library for Markdown parsing, while image processing is much faster in Go or Rust (e.g. about 500 ms vs 50 ms for that CPU-bound task). A monolith forces one language; microservices allow different languages per service.

### Costs of microservices

1. **The network:** a function call becomes a **network call** (HTTP or gRPC). That adds latency, and calls can **fail**, so you need retries, timeouts and failure handling.
2. **Harder debugging:** one request may pass through the load balancer, orders, payments and notifications services, so you need logs from all of them plus **distributed tracing** ([[Notes/Backend from First Principles/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability/18 Logging, Monitoring and Observability|lesson 18]]).
3. **Data consistency:** services often have their **own databases**, so you face replication lag and keeping data consistent across them.

### When to choose them

Consider microservices only with clear answers to: Do we have a **large team** whose boundaries match the service boundaries? Do parts need **independent scaling**? Do parts need **different technologies**? Otherwise, the complexity usually **outweighs** the benefits.

---

## 12. Serverless

Platforms such as **Vercel**, **Netlify** and **Cloudflare** have made **serverless** a popular way to scale.

### The traditional ("serverful") model

You rent a VM (e.g. AWS EC2) with an OS (e.g. Ubuntu), install your stack (nginx, Docker…), deploy your app, and **maintain the server** for its whole life. You know exactly what you have: e.g. 2 cores, 4 GB RAM, 30 GB SSD, 1 TB bandwidth/month.

Problems:

1. **Capacity planning:** you must **predict traffic** before launch.
   - **Under-provision** (e.g. 4 GB when you needed more): a spike makes the app slow (3–4 s responses) or crash, and users leave.
   - **Over-provision** (e.g. 32 GB when 8 GB was enough): you pay for unused capacity, e.g. $5,000 instead of $500 for the week.
2. **Autoscaling** helps by adding instances when usage crosses a threshold (e.g. 70% memory: two servers become three, and each drops to about 40%). But:
   - **it takes time:** booting an OS, fetching or building code, starting it, and registering with the load balancer can take seconds to minutes, too slow for a sudden burst,
   - **min/max limits:** a max that's too low brings back under-provisioning; a max that's too high risks a huge bill (e.g. $100,000 in a day during an attack or a big sale),
   - **it's reactive:** it scales only **after** load is detected, so you may already be overloaded.

   Autoscaling is still standard practice despite these limits.
3. **Always-on cost:** you pay for your minimum capacity 24/7, whether you get 500 requests per second or zero. That's fine for apps with **steady, predictable traffic** (most SaaS), but wasteful for spiky or rare workloads.

### What serverless means

There are still servers, but **you don't manage them**: no OS, no machine size, no server configuration. You provide:

1. **Functions** (your code), and
2. the **events** that trigger them (e.g. HTTP routes, queue messages).

A typical HTTP flow:

```text
request → API gateway (maps the route to a function) → provider runs your function on some machine → response
```

- On the first request, the provider (e.g. **AWS Lambda**, **Cloudflare Workers**) starts an instance with your code, runs it, and returns the response.
- Afterwards the instance may stay **warm** for a few seconds, or be pooled for reuse, before being shut down.
- **Pricing:** you pay only for the **time your code actually runs** (CPU and memory time), not 24/7.

### Trade-offs

1. **Cold starts:** the delay when no warm instance exists and a new one must start. This is serverless's biggest problem. Mitigations:
   - **keep-warm pings:** regularly call your own functions so an instance is always ready. Overdo it and you're paying 24/7 again, which defeats the point,
   - **fast runtimes:** the two big causes of cold starts are **booting a VM/OS** and **starting the language runtime**.
     - **AWS Firecracker**: lightweight KVM-based microVMs that boot very quickly, used for Lambda,
     - **Cloudflare Workers**: **V8 isolates** instead of VMs, near-instant start-up (Cloudflare claims around 0–5 ms),
     - language matters: runtimes like JavaScript/Node.js and Python start faster than ones with heavy startup like the JVM.

   Cold starts never fully disappear, because always-on servers are always ready.
2. **Execution limits:** e.g. an AWS Lambda invocation can run for **at most 15 minutes**, so a 30-minute job fails partway through.
3. **Statelessness:** instances come and go, so you can't rely on long-lived state such as persistent **TCP database connections** or **WebSocket** connections. These have to be rethought, e.g. with a **serverless database** or a pooler.

### When to use it

| Avoid serverless for | Good fits for serverless |
|---|---|
| **Latency-sensitive** user-facing apps (e.g. banking, payments) | **Occasional heavy jobs**: video/image processing, image resizing |
| **Long-running** requests or WebSocket connections | **Event-driven** work: a new queue message, a file upload, a database change |
| Apps needing **many DB connections** (without a serverless DB) | Spiky or rare workloads where always-on servers would sit idle |

In the creator's view, serverless is somewhat **overhyped**: a powerful tool for specific cases, not a universal replacement for servers.

---

## 13. Rules of thumb

Everything in these two lessons is a **solution**. Before reaching for any of them:

### 1. Start with the problem: measure first

- Is the system actually slow? **How** slow? **Which component**? What exactly is the bottleneck: a missing index? Lack of sharding?
- Use observability (logs, metrics, traces), profiling and **load testing**, with tools such as **Prometheus + Grafana** or a managed service like **New Relic**.
- Applying solutions without this is **premature optimization**. The worst outcome is **fixing the wrong bottleneck**: you think the problem is solved while the real one grows.

### 2. Prefer simple solutions

| Simpler | More complex |
|---|---|
| One large server (vertical scaling) | Horizontal scaling from day one / Kubernetes |
| Proper **indexes** | A Redis cache in front of every query |
| A **monolith** | Microservices |

**Complexity has a cost.** Every component can fail and must be monitored, understood and operated. Accept complexity only when simplicity is **genuinely insufficient**, and justify it.

### 3. Scale for the problems you have

Don't build for a million users on day one; most products never get there. Build for your current scale plus **reasonable headroom**. Generic advice from big-company engineering blogs (Netflix, Facebook, Google) may not fit your situation; your own measurements will tell you more.

### 4. Measure from day one

This is the exception to "keep it simple". Set up **production-grade observability** (logs, metrics, traces) from the start. You avoid mysterious errors and crashes, never have to guess where the bottleneck is, and get early warning to scale **before** problems hit users.

### 5. It's a mindset

As with [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/20 Backend Security/20 Backend Security|security]], performance and scaling are learned through **experience**: build, watch the system struggle, optimize, see what helps. The job isn't to predict every problem. It's to build systems that **handle problems gracefully** and to develop the skill to **measure, diagnose and resolve** them quickly.

---

## Key takeaways

- **Statelessness** enables horizontal scaling: keep sessions in Redis, files in object storage, and data in a central database.
- A **load balancer** distributes traffic: **round robin** (simple), **weighted**, **least connections** (adapts to slow requests), least response time, resource-based.
- **Health checks** remove dead instances from rotation and bring them back when they recover.
- Databases are the hard part. **Read replicas** offload reads but bring **replication lag**; **sharding** splits data across machines and depends on a good **shard key**.
- Prefer **managed/distributed databases** (RDS, Neon, PlanetScale, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB), but understand the concepts so you can configure them.
- **CDNs** beat distance (around 100 ms → 2–3 ms), reduce origin load and absorb **DDoS** attacks. **Edge computing** runs lightweight logic (auth, localisation) close to users.
- **Async processing** with queues and workers cuts perceived latency for emails, notifications, media processing and deletions.
- **Microservices** scale **teams**; they add network, debugging and consistency costs.
- **Serverless** removes server management and charges per use, but brings cold starts, execution limits and statelessness.
- **Measure first, keep it simple, scale for today, observe from day one.**

---

## Review questions

1. What does "stateless" mean for a backend server? How can you test whether your servers are stateless?
2. Explain the session bug with in-memory sessions and two instances. How does Redis fix it?
3. Where should files and application data live in a horizontally scaled system?
4. What does a load balancer do?
5. How does round robin work? When does it work well, and when does it fail?
6. What does weighted round robin add?
7. Walk through least connections with one 2-second request and several 200 ms requests.
8. Name two other load-balancing strategies.
9. What happens without health checks when an instance crashes? How do health checks fix this?
10. Why is the database harder to scale than the application servers?
11. How do read replicas work? What are their two main benefits?
12. What is replication lag? Describe the "renamed but still shows the old name" bug and three ways to handle it.
13. What is sharding? What two problems does it solve?
14. What is a shard key, and why is choosing one tricky?
15. What's the difference between partitioning and sharding?
16. Why is running your own database infrastructure discouraged? What do you still need to understand?
17. Why does a Tokyo user calling `us-east-1` always have at least about 100 ms of latency?
18. Give three benefits of CDNs. What content is typically cached on them?
19. How does a CDN help against DDoS attacks?
20. What's the difference between an edge node and edge computing? Give two good edge use cases.
21. Why can't everything run at the edge?
22. Explain the team-invite example. What latency does async processing save, and how is it built?
23. Why is deleting an account a good candidate for a background job?
24. What is a monolith? What are its strengths?
25. What problems do microservices solve, and for whom?
26. What are three costs of microservices?
27. What problems of the traditional server model does serverless address?
28. What are the limits of autoscaling?
29. What is a cold start? How do Firecracker and V8 isolates reduce it?
30. When should you avoid serverless, and when is it a good fit?
31. List the five rules of thumb from the end of the lesson.

## Source

- [21.2. Backend Scaling and Performance Engineering: Part-2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sOhAopEwjH4&list=PLui3EUkuMTPgZcV0QhQrOcwMPcBCcd_Q1). Written from the video's auto-generated transcript, following its teaching order. The provided transcript **ends mid-sentence** in the closing remarks.
- **Corrected names and terms:** Redis ("radius"), MinIO ("menu"), PostgreSQL ("posgress"), PlanetScale and Vitess ("pus"), Neon, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, CDNs ("cydians"), PoPs, Cloudflare Workers, V8 isolates, Upstash ("opt stash"), BullMQ ("bull mq"), RabbitMQ, Kafka, SendGrid, Mailchimp, Resend, nginx ("NX"), Vercel ("Versel"), Netlify ("Netleifi"), AWS Lambda, Firecracker, KVM, round robin ("roundroin"), least connections ("leash connections"), health checks ("L checks"), DDoS ("DOS").
- **Corrections and clarifications:**
  - The transcript says "centralized SQLite" for application data. SQLite is a file-based database tied to one machine, so the note lists a central server database (PostgreSQL, RDS) and uses SQLite as the example of what *not* to do.
  - The sharding example says "January to June" and "June to December"; the note uses January–June and July–December. The shard-key pitfalls (queries not using the key, hot shards) and the partitioning vs sharding distinction were added.
  - Neon is described in the transcript as "purely written in Rust"; its storage layer is written in Rust, while compute runs PostgreSQL.
  - AWS Lambda's limit is **at most** 15 minutes per invocation (the transcript says "at least").
  - Account-deletion timing: the transcript's "5 ms per table, 8 tables → 4 seconds" is internally inconsistent; the note keeps only the overall point (several seconds for large accounts).
  - The transcript says Cloudflare Workers "cannot do TCP"; the note says networking is restricted compared with a normal server, since newer Workers features allow some outbound TCP.
  - On cold starts, the note says JavaScript and Python runtimes "start faster" than the JVM rather than calling them purely interpreted, since modern JavaScript engines compile code at run time.
  - The note adds that the frontend "delay the refetch" workaround is not a guarantee, and that the load balancer marks failed instances unhealthy (the transcript says "blacklist").
- **Illustrative, not observed:** all numbers (200–300 ms vs 2 s requests, 8 GB vs 4 GB servers, 70%/30% read/write split, 200 ms replication lag, 20,000 km / 100 ms, 2–3 ms edge latency, 50% load reduction, 20,000 bots, $50,000 and $100,000 bills, 400 → 100 ms invite, 8 s deletion, 100–200 developers, 500 vs 50 ms image processing, $5,000 vs $500, 70% → 40% memory) are examples from the explanation. The diagrams and tables were written for this note. No live demo appears in this part.
- **The creator's opinions:** prefer managed databases over self-hosting; microservices scale teams more than machines and usually aren't worth it for small teams; serverless is "somewhat overhyped"; production-grade observability from day one always pays off. The creator's separate videos on CDNs and on serverless are mentioned but not covered here.
